extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of comedy/cultural/performance studies; theorists of humor; and interested comedians
extracted.subtask_description: Apply John Limon's 'abjection' lens to evaluate stand-up comedy: identify whether and how a joke or performance brings abject material to the stage and how audience response functions as communal exorcism. Emphasizes proximity to taboo and the balance between transgression and sheer disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the joke confront something abject?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the joke confront something abject?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central evaluative test in the Limon Lens: 'Funny stand-up forces the audience to confront something abject.' The abject includes bodily excretions and processes and psychic disowned material; confronting the abject is what produces the laugh as an act of expulsion. Anti-pattern: jokes that avoid abjection (sanitized, safe material) fail this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comedian expose something usually disowned?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comedian expose something usually disowned?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedian 'gives voice to what shouldn't be said' and 'brings the disowned to the stage.' Evaluate whether the performer explicitly names or embodies aspects of self/society that are typically repressed or denied. Guidance: assess clarity and courage of exposure and whether the exposure is framed to connect to shared identity or experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the audience implicated in the abjection?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the audience implicated in the abjection?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for whether the joke makes the audience a participant in the abjection rather than merely an observer — does the comic's framing invite the audience to recognize themselves as complicit or affected? Limon emphasizes communal exorcism: the laugh functions to expel the abject collectively. Scoring note: higher marks when the audience is clearly implicated and the laugh performs exorcism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the joke close enough to taboo to feel real?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke close enough to taboo to feel real?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proximity to taboo: 'Greatness = navigating closer to taboo without crossing into sheer disgust.' The ideal joke approaches or negotiates taboo territory so tension and recognition are felt; if it crosses into pure disgust, it fails. Scoring guidance: reward calibrated proximity to taboo; penalize both sanitization (too safe) and crossing into repellant disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the laughter expel rather than celebrate the abject?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the laughter expel rather than celebrate the abject?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the function of the laugh — according to Limon, laughter should perform expulsion of the abject (communal exorcism) rather than simply celebrating or endorsing the abject content. Consider whether the affective framing positions the audience to purge discomfort versus to fetishize or reward the abject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of abject material (what counts as 'abject')
rubrics_metrics.description: The abject includes: blood, feces, urine, vomit; bodily processes we'd rather disown; shame, embarrassment, awkwardness; the parts of self we deny but can't escape; the borders of 'I' and 'not-I.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to identify candidate material a joke might confront. This list functions as analytic vocabulary for auditors and performers to determine whether content qualifies as abject and how it might be mobilized on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern — sanitized, safe material (evading the abject)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad stand-up evades the abject (sanitized, safe).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limon treats sanitized or overtly safe material as a fail: it does not produce the necessary confrontation or communal exorcism. In scoring or critique, mark such material down for avoiding the abject; consider whether apparent 'safety' results from cultural privilege that excludes other voices from abject labor.
